On the night Ramchandra Ray escapes, Udayaditya is the armed, active rescuer and Sitaram the obedient guard. Udayaditya kicks on the locked inner-quarters door and orders it opened. Sitaram with folded hands says he has orders that no one leave that night, but he cannot take up arms against the Yubaraj because the Yubaraj has saved his life twice, and he touches the dust of his feet. He then asks Udayaditya not to destroy the life he saved - to take his weapon and bind him head to foot with his own cloth, so he will have an excuse before the Maharaj the next day. Udayaditya disarms him, ties him and leaves him lying there, then jumps the high wall, falls on the sleeping guard there, snatches his weapon, ties him, takes his key and opens the outer door, telling that guard also to say the Yubaraj overpowered them by force.

On the night of Udayaditya's own escape the agency is inverted. Udayaditya is the unarmed, weakened prisoner sitting alone in the dark after his lamp goes out, long confined and without will or direction. Sitaram comes to him, announces the prison is on fire and to come out quickly, then grabs him and almost carries him out into the open field. Where Udayaditya had previously demanded and applied force, he now asks helplessly what he should do and where he should go, and Sitaram answers authoritatively to come with him and leads him. The fire that empties the guard posts - the guards at his door who had guarded only from custom flee first - provides the cover for the escape, so Sitaram no longer needs to be staged as a victim of force but instead actively creates the diversion and rescues the prince, repaying the life-debt he had invoked on the first night.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was to have two Pathan assassins murder Basanta Ray while he was en route to Jessore, when he took shelter at the inn at Simultali — one Pathan was to lure Basanta Ray's retainers away by falsely crying that dacoits had attacked a village, while the other killed the isolated old king. The plan failed because the Pathan assigned to kill him was moved by Basanta Ray's kindness and music, could not carry out the deed, and instead confessed the plot to Basanta Ray and Udayaditya and begged for refuge.

The plan that succeeded was a formal execution by military force. Pratapaditya issued a signed death warrant for the King of Raigarh and sent a large force under Muktiyar Khan, who first captured Udayaditya in a field outside Raigarh, then had his soldiers shed their uniforms, hide their weapons and enter the fort in plain clothes through its many gates. After surrounding Basanta Ray as he finished his evening prayers and presenting the handwritten order, Muktiyar had his man Abdul behead/cut down the old king with a drawn sword inside the palace prayer room.

First, in the inner quarters of the Jessore palace — in the Mahishi's room while feeding servants — disguised as a middle-aged woman after mocking the palace ladies and the Mahishi, where Rammohan seized his hands, tore off his head-cloth, lifted and swung him overhead, seized him by the throat and tied him in a shawl and carried him out over his shoulder like a sack.

Second, in the king's room of the Ramchandra Ray's palace at Chandradwip while present as the court jester Ramai Bhand after insulting Vibha, the princess/Mahishi of Jessore, with a sly remark, where Rammohan forcibly grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and threw him out of the room — threatening to have his head shaved, pour whey over it and drive him from the city.

Surma does not depart for her father's house — the Rajmahishi, with Pratapaditya's consent to delay the exile, secretly sends Matangini to fetch a tantra-mantra medicine from the widow Mangala who is Rukmini to win Udayaditya's heart back, and Mangala spends five days preparing a poison which Surma ingests, dying in Udayaditya's lap on the eve of her departure.

Vibha's refusal to return with Rammohan is taken as a grave insult to Ramchandra Ray and his dynasty. Wounded in honor and egged on by his court, Ramchandra decides to take another wife to avenge the slight. When Vibha later arrives in Chandradwip and reaches the palace, she learns that on that very day Ramchandra is getting married and that there is no longer any place or home for her in her own kingdom and royal palace.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya's signet ring by entering his bedchamber during a storm, playing on his guilt and pity and demanding the ring from his finger, which he pulls off and throws to her. She gives the ring to Sitaram, and Sitaram and Rukmini conspire with Bhagavat to forge a petition to the Emperor in which Udayaditya appears to accuse Pratapaditya of treason to gain the kingdom for himself, stamping it with the seal engraved with Udayaditya's name from the ring. Bhagavat is entrusted to deliver it to Delhi but instead takes it to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted a servant of Udayaditya carrying it to Delhi and that the servant fled, without naming Sitaram. Pratapaditya uses the sealed document as pretext to order Udayaditya imprisoned under guard, even while admitting he does not fully believe it.

The midnight escape required Udayaditya to force open the locked inner quarters - disarming Sitaram after Sitaram pleaded to be tied up to avoid punishment, and overpowering a second guard at the outer wall to take his key.

For failing to enforce the order that no one leave the inner quarters that night, Sitaram and Bhagavat were dismissed without pay, leaving their families destitute.

Udayaditya, stating that punishing them was punishing him because they were punished for yielding to him, fixed a monthly stipend for them. When Pratapaditya learned of this he forbade any further help, regarding Udayaditya's mercy as defiance of his own cruelty and authority.

Udayaditya and Surma continued the help secretly to avoid displeasing Pratapaditya openly - Surma arranged for a trusted maid to deliver the money to Sitaram's mother and Bhagavat's wife. The maid confided in Mangala, through whom the secret reached Pratapaditya.

Unable to punish Udayaditya directly and unable to use physical force in the inner quarters, Pratapaditya retaliated indirectly by ordering Surma to be sent to her paternal home, enforced through the Mahishi, as punishment for defying his ban and to remove her supportive influence on Udayaditya.

The song "I alone am left behind" is Basanta Ray's lament of old age, survival and utter loneliness — that what was there has gone away and only emptiness/illusion remains, that those who were once his no longer answer his call, leaving him to ask with whom and with what spirit he can go on living.

He sings it in two contrasting contexts:

**1. In Raigarh, alone on the veranda at sunset -** as a spontaneous, pensive, almost poetic humming to himself while gazing at the setting sun beyond the field and mango grove. His sitar is with him but its strings are broken and cannot be tuned. The song arises from a wistful, abstract melancholy — the feeling that he still sings but those he used to sing for are no longer there, that joy arises but there is no one left to embrace, an anticipatory sense of emptiness.

**2. In Jessore, in the inner quarters of the palace -** as a heart-rending, realized grief after hearing of Udayaditya's imprisonment and arriving to find the household dark and desolate. After seeing Vibha alone - the sole broken remnant of the happy family - and standing at the door of the silent, empty, dark room where sounds of joy once arose and finding no one inside, he stands silently for a long time, takes Vibha's hand and slowly sings the same line. Here the abstract lament has become literal and shared - the emptiness is no longer a mood but the actual desolation of the family, with the beloved grandsons scattered, one in prison, and the house crying out "those who were here before are here no more."

Rukmini tried to physically stop the escape at the canal by leaping on Udayaditya but was blocked by Sitaram, was separated by the boatmen, and in rage jumped into the high monsoon water uttering a curse. She survived and returned.

Sitaram had created a cover by setting fire to the empty prison cell, throwing bones, a skull and Udayaditya's sword inside and collapsing the roof, so that guards and Pratapaditya would believe Udayaditya had died screaming in the fire.

Rukmini went directly to Pratapaditya's assembly and contradicted that story, telling him the Yubaraj had not died but had escaped by boat with the old King of Raigarh through Sitaram's conspiracy, and reproaching the guards for ignoring her warning the night before when she told them the Yubaraj was escaping. On her offer to find them herself, Pratapaditya gave her armed men.

Her party tracked Udayaditya to Raigarh and confirmed he was there, and she remained in Raigarh. On that information Pratapaditya gave Muktiyar Khan a secret written order for the death sentence of the King of Raigarh.

In Raigarh, it was Rukmini who guided the soldiers to Udayaditya as he walked alone in the field at dusk, crying out to identify him, allowing Muktiyar Khan to surround and capture him. With Udayaditya detained and prevented from warning his grand-uncle, Muktiyar Khan was able to enter the fort in disguise while Basanta Ray was at evening prayer, present Pratapaditya's signed death order, and have him executed.

Pratapaditya's initial reception is one of calculated cold indifference and dismissal intended to assert superiority. He makes no festive preparations - no lit path or Nabat playing - sends only the Dewan with 250 men to meet Ramchandra well beyond the usual point at Chakdihi and provides a small elephant, and when Ramchandra arrives he remains seated with his minister, offers only a calm "Come. Are you well?", then ignores him to read a long document concerning a tax collector, interrupts Ramchandra's attempt to answer about floods, and finally dismisses him with "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters."

In his own court, Ramchandra inverts this hierarchy through active, public denigration. Seated on his throne smoking his hookah, he presides over daily sessions where his minister, Dewan and jester Ramai Bhand empty their quivers of verbal arrows against Pratapaditya's back to his visible pleasure. They mock Pratapaditya's lineage as only two generations old - his grandfather an earthworm, his father a leech bloated on subjects' blood, himself a hooded snake - and claim Pratapaditya's father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather for anointment with the little toe of his left foot, portraying Ramchandra's house as ancient and superior. Where Pratapaditya asserted dominance through silent neglect, Ramchandra seeks revenge through loud, flatterer-driven ridicule.

She is Rukmini, the lone widow three years older than Udayaditya who lived in Raigarh under Basanta Ray's grace and lured him when he was eighteen, an episode he confesses to Surma with lasting shame. She leaves Raigarh, changes her name to Mangala and settles on the outskirts of Jessore, keeping palace servants in her pay and watching for news of the palace while hoping to rule Jessore through the Yubaraj's heart and performing rites for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma.

She re-enters when the Rajmahishi, wanting to win the Yubaraj's heart back from Surma before sending Surma away, hears Mangala knows tantra and medicine and sends Matangini to secretly fetch a draught from her. Mangala spends five nights cutting, soaking, grinding and mixing roots and chanting mantras to prepare a poison - prepared to appear as a love medicine and to make the Yubaraj feel no pity when Surma dies - which is then given to Surma. On the eve of Surma's planned departure from the palace Surma collapses with cold limbs and labored breathing and dies in the night, with the palace putting out that she died by her own hand having taken poison. After Surma's death Mangala again enters Udayaditya's life directly, coming uninvited by lamplight into his dark bedchamber during a storm while he holds a sleeping child, reproaching him for ruining her and demanding his love and his ring.

In his early lament to Surma, Udayaditya says he desires no happiness and wishes he had not been born in a royal palace as the crown prince and sole heir to the throne, wealth, honor and glory of Jessore. He feels he was born only as an heir, not as a son - his father Pratapaditya has tested him at every moment with the eyes of an examiner to see if he can bear the burden of the kingdom, while relatives, ministers and subjects scrutinize him and dismiss him as a fool. He cites the proof of his unfitness when at sixteen he was given charge of the Hosenkhali pargana and within six months revenue fell and disorder arose, leading the court to conclude his popularity with subjects proved he could never rule and earning his father's contempt and comparison to his uncle Basanta Ray of Raigarh who would play sitar and ruin the kingdom. He asks what penance could reverse this birth.

This culminates when, after being brought as a prisoner before Pratapaditya, he is asked what punishment is fitting. He answers whatever the king commands and agrees he is not worthy of the kingdom and does not want it, begging release from the throne. Pressed on the sincerity of this, he declares he has never lied for gain and offers to swear touching the feet of Ma-Kali in the temple that as long as he lives he will not accept even a needle's tip of Jessore, will not sit on its throne nor touch its scepter, and if he does may the sin of his grand-uncle's murder be his. Pratapaditya accepts, and Udayaditya asks only not to be locked in a cell like a caged beast but to be abandoned to leave at once for Kashi, requesting only some money to establish a guest house and temple there in his grand-uncle's name, with Samaraditya to be heir to the kingdom.

Ramchandra Ray, wounded in self-esteem and wanting to turn the insult back on Pratapaditya, writes a letter renouncing Vibha and stating she should not be sent to Chandradwip again. He first asks Rammohan to deliver it to Jessore, but Rammohan refuses. He then entrusts it to the old Nayanchand. Nayanchand, afraid of what Pratapaditya would do if the letter reached him, does not deliver it to the Maharaj but gives it privately to the Mahishi.

The Mahishi is overwhelmed — fearing Vibha would not survive the blow if told, and fearing disaster if the Maharaj learned of it — and hides the letter from both of them. She weeps before Pratapaditya only hinting hypothetically about what if a son-in-law were to abandon Vibha, without revealing the letter exists. Later she confides in Basanta Ray and shows him the letter.

Basanta Ray, stunned, advises her to show it to no one else and to send Vibha to her in-laws' house at once without concern for honor or dishonor, reasoning that Ramchandra wrote out of anger and the anger would subside once she returns. To ensure Vibha goes willingly and happily, he instructs that it be announced in the household as the opposite of its true content — that Ramchandra has written requesting Vibha be sent to Chandradwip. The Mahishi follows this advice and tells Vibha and the whole household that a letter has arrived from Ramchandra asking for Vibha to be sent, which Vibha receives with immense joy, believing her husband has forgiven and lovingly summoned her.

Pratapaditya ordered the canal adjoining the palace where Ramchandra Ray's sixty-four-oared boat was moored to be blocked with large logs of sal wood and had all doors leading out of the inner quarters locked. The escape party bypassed the locked doors by lowering Ramchandra from the palace roof, about seventy cubits above the canal, on a rope made of thick sheets tied to a pillar, with Rammohan carrying him on his back and then lowering him into the boat. When the boat was stopped by the logs, the guards could not stop it - their stones did not reach, they had swords but no ready guns, and while they searched for gunpowder and bullets the crew pulled the boat up and over the logs. The guards' pursuit boat was then delayed because the man sent to fetch it stopped to smoke and collect a debt, and the subsequent scolding delayed them further, allowing the boat to reach the Bhairav river and escape.

His sitar is his eternal companion and embodiment of his joy, and its fate mirrors his inner collapse as he is torn from Udayaditya. At the moment of forced parting he tries to use it as a shield against grief — picking it up and playing furiously with great clatter to drown out the weeping around him — but tears blur his eyes, his throat chokes and words fail, forcing him to stop and put it down. He then renounces it entirely, leaving it behind with Udayaditya and declaring he will not play it anymore, a voluntary abandonment of music and happiness because the grandson for whom he played is being taken away. Later in lonely exile he is seen without it, gazing at the sunset and humming joylessly about being left alone with only emptiness remaining. When asked where the instrument is, he says it still exists but its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned — an image of himself, untunable and broken, unable to produce any joy without his loved ones. The progression from hindered, tear-interrupted playing to deliberate abandonment to a broken, untunable instrument reflects a deepening despair from painful separation to utter desolation.

Earlier Udayaditya was known for involving himself in the affairs of the subjects and acting against his father's wishes, treating danger as a trifle and fighting against oppression with all his might without considering consequences.

After Surma's death a blind fear of Pratapaditya takes hold, his former courage is gone and he hesitates in every task with doubt in every matter. When he hears an order has been given to loot and burn the estate office of the zamindar of Chhapra he has his horse readied and then cancels it saying nowhere to go; when he sees a royal official beating a subject tied to a tree who cries to him for mercy he cannot bear it but runs inside his house instead of stopping the official as he would have before; and when the stipends for Bhagavat and Sitaram are stopped he no longer has the courage to help them openly or secretly, resolving to send money but hesitating until it is never sent.

Sitaram had conspired with Bhagavat to forge a petition in the Yubaraj's name accusing Pratapaditya of treason before the Emperor, using the Yubaraj's seal, which Bhagavat then delivered to Pratapaditya and which caused Pratapaditya to have Udayaditya imprisoned. Sitaram undoes this by arranging a fire in the row of guard huts near the prison to create a panic and cause the guards to desert their posts, then opening Udayaditya's dark cell, telling him the prison is on fire, and forcibly carrying him out to the open field outside to escape.

On one occasion Rammohan rescues Ramchandra Ray from the locked inner quarters of Pratapaditya's Jessore palace. After Udayaditya forces the locked doors and brings Ramchandra to him, Rammohan has thick sheets twisted together into a huge rope, tied to a small pillar on the palace roof on the side above the canal about seventy cubits below where Ramchandra's sixty-four-oared boat is moored. With the rope ending a little above the boat, he lifts Ramchandra onto his back, Ramchandra clinging with closed eyes, and climbs down hand over hand. At the end of the rope he grips it with his teeth, releases Ramchandra from his back and lowers him very carefully with both hands into the boat before jumping down himself.

On the other occasion he rescues Vibha from Ramchandra's palace in Chandradwip after she is publicly repudiated and faints. He lifts the unconscious, trembling Vibha from the floor, carries her out of the room and palace, and places her into one of the palanquins waiting near the gate to return her to the boat, afterwards taking her to Kashi.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as an ornate royal bride for Ramchandra's reception, despite her own preference for simplicity. Against her wish for three thin turquoise bangles on each delicate hand, she is made to wear eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring unsuited to her small face, and an elaborate, heavy coiffure redone by her mother after she had it styled simply to her own liking. She is displayed to the household carrying the burden of excessive jewelry and adornment, flushed with shy joy.

In Chandradwip, she deliberately rejects all royal markers. She refuses a palanquin, declaring she will go not as a queen but as a common subject and beggar-woman, and leaves the boat dressed as a common woman. She enters the palace like a maidservant, unrecognized and unwelcomed, her veil slipped, to the point that the king mistakes her for a beggar woman seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma's death the window is a symbol of absence and mourning. He sits at it leaving the place where Surma used to sit deliberately empty, looking out at the same moonlight, garden and breeze as before and haunted by the sense that she should still be there, waiting vainly for her return and experiencing the window as a reminder of half his life being gone.

In the prison cell the window, a very small opening showing only a sliver of sky, bamboo grove, temple and passing birds, becomes the opposite — a symbol of natural freedom, hope and spiritual liberation. He refuses the bed and sits on the floor against the casement, saying that only by looking at the sky and watching birds fly can he believe his cage will one day break and he will swim in the endless sky; the small space by the window is the only place where no king can hold him captive, while the soft bed inside the room has become the true prison.

Initially the relationship is a flirtatious transaction: Rukmini, a widow who lives by lending at interest and controlling men through beauty and money, and Sitaram, a penniless but boastful palace guard, maintain a playful patronage. He comes when he needs cash, reciting love-verse and begging for gold and silver while claiming his mother who keeps his money is away and he will repay tomorrow; she gives the money with feigned affection, laughing to herself that it will never be returned and telling him he can pay whenever convenient. Their exchange becomes overtly amorous and comic, with him calling her Subhadra and himself Jagannath, arguing over the myth of Subhadra's abduction, and repeating pet names — Pran, Priye, Priyatame, Pranpriye — at her prompting, then pretending to be hurt when she feigns offense at his question about interest.

That bantering dependence turns into secret conspiracy, as they are seen conferring together privately and Sitaram says they will need Bhagavat's help to carry out a scheme.

The break comes with Udayaditya's imprisonment. Sitaram goes to Rukmini's house and reviles her, threatening to set her house on fire, grind her face on the stone floor, smear it with lime and soot and drive her from the city, and then leaves to free the Yubaraj. She answers with convulsive rage — clenched teeth, tightened fists, trembling body — declaring the Yubaraj is hers alone, that only she can help or harm him, and that she will see how he manages to free him.

Finally it becomes murderous. After engineering a widespread fire to fake Udayaditya's death in his cell — planting bones, a skull and the prince's sword in the flames — Sitaram decides on his flight to also rob Rukmini, reasoning she is ruined, has no kin, has much money, and that if he does not take it someone else will. He enters her open, dark cottage at night and finds her alive, soaked, hair dripping, teeth chattering, sitting silent in faint lamplight after returning, as she says, from the door of Yama. She vows to lay him and the Yubaraj in an oven and smear their pyre-ash on her body before Yama will have her. He again tries feigned sweetness and soft words, which only inflames her; she seizes a curved blade to kill him, striking the floor where he had stood after he slips out and flees Jessore that night, while she becomes openly reckless, driving away all who approach.

Sitaram's fire begins as a distraction to remove the guards and extract Udayaditya — a blaze is set in the long row of guard huts near the prison where their belongings are kept, causing the guards, including those at Udayaditya's door who were only guarding by custom, to abandon their posts. Amid the cries of "Fire! Fire!" and the rush of footsteps, Sitaram opens the prison door, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and carries him out to the open field.

It then becomes a sustained diversion and a fabricated death: the fire was not accidental but set simultaneously in five or six rooms by Sitaram with loyal commoners and palace servants, and his men among the fire-fighters sabotage the extinguishing — pouring water where there is no fire, not bringing water back, breaking pots and creating confusion — so the fire does not go out. While the chaos continues his men set fire to Udayaditya's now-empty cell, burning windows, doors, beams and fences, and Sitaram plants bones, a skull and Udayaditya's sword inside. Staged shouts that the Yubaraj's cell has caught fire, that his screams were heard and that the roof has collapsed with no response, prevent anyone from entering, and later the burnt, melted remains of the sword and witness testimony that the Yubaraj was seen and heard screaming in the flames are presented to create the cover story that he died in the fire.

Despite Udayaditya having risked his own life to force open the locked inner quarters, overpower guards, and arrange Ramchandra's escape down a rope from the roof to the boat, Ramchandra later shows no gratitude in his own court. He treats the rescue as something that was bound to happen and that anyone would have done for him, believing the world should naturally unite to save him if even a thorn pricked his foot, and deciding he himself outweighs the whole world in importance. He rationalizes that Udayaditya did not save him for his own sake but for his sister Vibha's sake, so the act deserves no thanks. For the crime of being Pratapaditya's son, he allows Udayaditya's name to be brought up for laughter and joins the minister and jester Ramai Bhand in daily mockery and ridicule of Pratapaditya and Udayaditya, lacking the mental strength to refrain or to stop the others for fear of what they would think of him.

Initially Pratapaditya treats warnings about the Emperor of Delhi's displeasure over the planned murder of his paternal uncle Basanta Ray as cowardice and insult. When the minister warns that the Emperor's anger means fifty thousand soldiers and that killing Basanta Ray will lead to opposition and excommunication, Pratapaditya declares the Emperor is not his God, that others like Mansingh, Birbal and Basanta Ray may tremble before him but he will not, and forbids the minister to utter the Emperor's name until the killing is accomplished. He similarly dismisses a later warning that a complaint has already been lodged against him with the Emperor, saying he himself will judge and punish the Emperor.

That specter of appealing to Delhi is later weaponized internally against his son, Prince Udayaditya. Bhagavat and Sitaram conspire to forge a petition made to appear as if Udayaditya himself is lodging a complaint of treason against his father with the Emperor to obtain the kingdom for himself. Using the ring bearing the Yubaraj's seal that Rukmini had brought, they stamp the forged document with his name. Bhagavat does not take it to Delhi but delivers it directly to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted a servant of Udayaditya carrying it to the Dillishwar who had then fled. The presentation of his son as a traitor secretly invoking the Emperor's power enrages Pratapaditya and provides the pretext for turning against and imprisoning Udayaditya, while Bhagavat is restored to his position.

Vibha's hair is a marker of her bond with Surma. When Surma is present, Vibha trusts only her to style her hair to her own taste — secretly having Surma redo the elaborate coiffure imposed by her mother, which her mother then undoes and re-styles, accusing Surma of jealousy — showing Surma as Vibha's intimate confidante against maternal adornment. After Surma is gone, the daily ritual becomes an emblem of absence: at the time for braiding, Vibha sits quietly waiting for Surma to come and braid it, and when evening falls without her, her hair remains unbraided. Later, her unkempt, neglected hair, noted as having dark circles under her eyes and no smile, signals that there is no one left in the palace to care for her.
